newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Far-flung Chechens return to vote.
newsitem.headline: Far-flung Chechens return to vote.

text.p: "This is my country," said Marina, flying in to Grozny on Friday for the first time in two years. "Russia tried to destroy it. Now it's my duty to come back and take part in deciding our independent future."

The last time she was in Chechnya, this well-dressed store manager and mother in her late 30s spent some long terrifying moments cowering on the floor of a bus, showered with glass as it was raked by automatic fire from Russian police commandos.

That was last August, when the Russian army gave the people of the regional capital Grozny 48 hours to flee or be bombed in their homes as Moscow's forces struggled to turn the tables on Chechen guerrillas who had seized the city.

It turned out to be the last, hollow gesture of a defeated power. The then Kremlin security chief, General Alexander Lebed, stepped in to make a peace that saw the last Russian soldier leave Chechnya last month and will culminate on Monday in the region's first internationally-monitored election.

It is an event Marina says she did not want to miss. After the battle of Grozny in August, when she lost her house for a second time in the 21-month war, she moved her children to Moscow so they could go to school. Their own was destroyed.
So she was flying back to vote -- the first time she has flown direct since Grozny airport was closed by the war.

Yet like many in this mainly Moslem Caucasus region of one million, Marina is no wild-eyed fanatic. As a professional woman, she is not anxious to see strict Islamic law develop in Chechnya. She has travelled abroad, last year to Italy.

And she confesses to little initial sympathy for Dzhokhar Dudayev, the Soviet general who returned as the Soviet Union broke up to lead his people into a de facto independence in 1991 that finally brought down Moscow's wrath upon them.
"When he held his parades and rallies, I wasn't interested. We didn't want to go to war," she said, in the soft, barely accented Russian of Grozny's urban educated classes.

But Russia's heavy-handed intervention, which killed tens of thousands of Chechens including Dudayev, has hardened this ordinary Soviet citizen -- she even has a Russian forename -- into a bitter anti-Moscow nationalist, leaving her children to come and vote for one of 16 presidential candidates, all of them pledged to fulfill Dudayev's dream of full independence.

Up to half a million people may vote on January 27, but many, perhaps hundreds of thousands including ethnic Russians living as refugees outside Chechnya, will be unable to take part -- a fact Moscow says makes the election unfair.

But Marina said three centuries of conflict, since tsarist Russia first started to expand into the Caucasus, had done nothing but harm to the Chechen people. Now it was time to go it alone, without following Moscow's orders, she added.
"(Russians) are not like us. They don't like to work, they just get drunk, they envy people who have some success. And they hate us," she said. "So why should we live by their laws."

The prospect of going it alone is daunting, however. Much of Grozny, including Marina's home and the city centre store where she was assistant manager, lies in ruins as do the oil refineries that once assured the city's prosperity.
"It's hard to imagine how we can rebuild. Whatever happens the war has left its scars on all of us, the children have had no education," Marina said. "It's going to be very hard work."
